claims.text: A machine-learning interatomic potential can reproduce ab initio solid and liquid free energies for CoCrFeNi near melting.
Using the machine-learning potential would substantially reduce the computational cost of evaluating CoCrFeNi fusion thermodynamics.
The target system includes both solid and liquid CoCrFeNi over approximately 0.9–1.1 Tm.
The proposed potential will be a moment-tensor or neural-network potential trained on short ab initio molecular-dynamics trajectories and force–displacement calculations.
Curating a high-quality training dataset is important to machine-learning accuracy.
Augmenting the training set with configurations and observables sensitive to electron–vibration coupling will ensure that this coupling is captured.
The learned surrogate potential-energy surface will represent anharmonic interactions and electron–vibration effects across the fusion transition.
Replacing extensive AIMD sampling with sampling driven by the learned potential will reduce computational expense.
The learned potential will retain ab initio accuracy for the entropy and free-energy contributions needed on both sides of melting.
Targeted electron–vibration-sensitive training will allow the model to reproduce complex energy landscapes and vibrational behavior.
The surrogate will enable efficient free-energy integration across the solid–liquid phase boundary.
The proposed method will be 10–100 times faster than explicit AIMD.
The proposed method will be 10–100 times faster than TOR-TILD.
Predicted fusion temperature, latent heat, entropy contributions, and phase free energies will fall within experimental uncertainty.
AIMD can produce finite-temperature vibrational entropies in good agreement with experiment for elemental solids.
Simulation-based entropy methods can in principle include anharmonic contributions beyond thermal expansion.
TOR-TILD requires extensive computational resources and long molecular-dynamics trajectories to capture anharmonicity and electron–vibration interactions.
The hypothesis is falsified if phase free energies or derived observables differ from explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD benchmarks by more than approximately 5–10%.
